summary: This informational document defines Brotli, a lossless compressed data format that combines LZ77 with Huffman coding, with efficiency comparable to the best general-purpose compression methods available. The specification describes the format of the compressed data stream. It is widely used for compressing web content.

plainLanguage.summary: Brotli is a format for reducing the size of data without losing any information. It records literal bytes and instructions to copy earlier text, then defines how a decoder reconstructs the original stream.

subtitle: A lossless compressed data format built from backward copies, prefix codes, and a static dictionary.

tldr.problem: Software needs a portable, lossless format for compressing byte streams that can be decoded across different systems.
tldr.mechanism: Brotli divides a stream into meta-blocks and encodes literal bytes and backward copies using prefix codes, with optional references to a static dictionary.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7932 specifies valid Brotli streams and a decoding algorithm, and registers br as an HTTP content coding. It is updated by RFC 9841.

today: RFC 7932 is an Informational RFC published in July 2016. It is updated by RFC 9841.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope of the Format
sections.content:
The specification defines a lossless format that is independent of processor type, operating system, file system, and character set. It is intended for sequential streams and uses a bounded amount of intermediate storage. The format does not aim to provide random access or to outperform specialized compression methods on specialized data.

RFC 7932 defines which compressed streams are valid and gives a decoder algorithm for recovering the original byte stream. The RFC also states that Brotli is part of the WOFF File Format 2.0.
sections.plainLanguage: The format lets software compress and restore a stream of bytes without changing its contents. The same format can be handled on different kinds of computers.

sections.title: Streams, Meta-Blocks, and Copies
sections.content:
A compressed stream begins with a header and continues with meta-blocks. Each meta-block produces up to 16,777,216 uncompressed bytes, and the decoded output is the blocks joined together. The header specifies a sliding window, which tells the decoder how much earlier output it must retain.

Compressed data is represented as commands that insert literal bytes and copy a sequence from earlier output. A copy uses a length and backward distance. A reference may instead point to an entry in the static dictionary. A meta-block may also carry uncompressed bytes directly or be empty and contain metadata.
sections.plainLanguage: The decoder reads a sequence of blocks. Within a compressed block, commands either add new bytes or copy bytes that appeared earlier.

sections.title: Prefix Codes and Context
sections.content:
Brotli uses canonical prefix codes for literal bytes, insert-and-copy lengths, and distances. A prefix code represents symbols with bit sequences that a decoder can read unambiguously. The code descriptions are stored in compact form in each meta-block header.

For literals, the selected code can depend on the previous two uncompressed bytes. Distance codes can depend on the copy length. The format also includes a static dictionary of words and defined transformations of those words, allowing some repeated text to be represented by a dictionary reference.
sections.plainLanguage: Short codes represent common symbols, and the format can select different codes based on nearby data. A built-in dictionary also lets a stream refer to a word instead of spelling it out.

sections.title: Headers and Decoding
sections.content:
The stream header gives the sliding-window size. Each meta-block header gives its uncompressed length and describes its coding information, including block types and prefix codes. The decoder reads commands until it has produced the number of bytes specified for that block.

The specification requires invalid data to be rejected, including streams that end before the last meta-block is complete. Backward references cannot reach before the start of the stream or beyond the permitted window; references outside those limits identify dictionary entries.
sections.plainLanguage: Each block’s header tells the decoder how much output to produce and how to interpret the codes that follow. A decoder rejects streams that violate the format or end before the final block is complete.

sections.title: Security and HTTP Registration
sections.content:
Decompressors should bounds-check memory accesses and check the declared window and uncompressed block sizes. Otherwise, malformed or oversized input could cause memory errors or use resources out of proportion to the compressed data. The RFC also warns that combining attacker-controlled data and secrets in one compressed stream, then exposing encrypted output lengths, can reveal information about the secrets.

The RFC registers br as the name for Brotli in the HTTP Content Coding Registry.
sections.plainLanguage: A decoder needs to check sizes and memory access when handling compressed input. Applications should keep secret data separate from data an attacker can choose when compressing content for encryption.
